1:
Augustine explains that Luke, having finished the denial of Peter, went back over the morning and laid open the charges falsely brought, where Matthew and Mark say only that they accused him. Bede sees the delivery to Pilate as fulfilling the word that he should be given to the Gentiles. Cyril of Alexandria's comment here still stands on the night before, over which he sets Jeremiah's wish for a fountain of tears. Henry calls the move to Pilate impotent malice, since having condemned him as a blasphemer they knew they could not put him to death, and so charged him not with blasphemy, which the governor did not try, but with disaffection to a government they themselves resented; Robertson notes the same want of power, which is why they say nothing of their own sentence.

Robertson counts three charges and observes that not one gives their real reason, while Henry finds the indictment a pretended zeal for Caesar, and remarks that the crime falsely charged was the one for which Rome soon after destroyed them. He calls the second a flat untruth, their brightest students having tried to make Jesus say that very thing and failed, and grants the third true though not in the sense meant, since Pilate would make little of the word Christ but had to notice a king. Theophylact answers from the other side, that so far from forbidding tribute he commanded it paid, and that a man who fled when the multitude would have crowned him can hardly have sought a kingdom. Clarke calls them the falsest slanders that could be invented, notes that several copies of the Itala add the destroying of the law and the prophets, and that neither Christ nor any follower ever forbade lawful taxes.

Lightfoot supplies a rabbinic phrase behind the first charge, that to corrupt one's food publicly meant mingling true doctrine with heresy, in a Talmudic sentence naming Jesus which the Aruch cites more cautiously with Jeroboam. Ellicott finds Luke's report more definite than the others, traces the charge to the earlier question about tribute, and notes that the Greek speaks of taxes generally where that was of the poll-tax alone. Bede suggests that Pilate, having heard the saying about rendering to Caesar, set that charge aside as a palpable lie and asked only about the kingdom. Theophylact hears derision in it, as though a poor and naked man were accused of seeking a kingdom needing many helpers and much money.

Robertson notes that all four Gospels give Pilate's question in the same words and that the answer is a real affirmative, as Ellicott presses too. Augustine reads it as deliberate, the governor answered in the words used to the chief priests so that he might be condemned out of his own mouth, Tertullian that he said no more lest he seem driven by fear. Tertullian sets the scene under the second psalm: the heathen were Pilate and the Romans, the people the tribes of Israel, the kings represented in Herod and the rulers in the chief priests. Calvin gives the reason for the trial itself, that since Christ came to bear our punishment it was proper he should first be condemned by the mouth of his judge.

On the acquittal Barnes and Clarke agree that Pilate found no evidence of the crime charged, and Robertson that Luke leaves the examination to John, Pilate having taken Jesus inside and come out again to the Sanhedrin, who would not enter. Wesley notes that the verdict followed a hearing, Gill that the priests would not accept it. Theophylact says that, having nothing else to support the calumny, they had recourse to clamour, and that Galilee was named to alarm Pilate, the Galileans being given to sedition. Bede answers that with these words they accuse not him but themselves, and Cyril of Jerusalem bids us not be ashamed of the Cross.
6:
Bede reads Pilate's question as relief rather than inquiry, since he was glad of any opening that let him escape sentence and preferred that the tetrarch of our Lord's own country should judge him; the catena appends that this followed the Roman rule by which a man was tried by the governor of his own jurisdiction. Ellicott says the same, that Pilate caught at the word in hope of shifting the responsibility for condemning one he believed innocent, while lacking the courage to acquit him. Lightfoot asks whether a capital jurisdiction was being conceded inside Jerusalem, and answers that Pilate acted to flatter the tetrarch or to throw off the odium. Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson agree that Galilee lay under Herod, and Ellicott adds that the tetrarch kept a court at the Passover with his own rabbis and troops.

Ellicott suggests that this incident, peculiar to Luke, reached him from Manaen or others of the Herodian household. Gregory says Herod wished to make proof of Christ's fame and witness his miracles, while Calvin turns the gladness into a portrait of the flesh, which would see God in his works without submitting to his authority. He presses it further, that Herod, who reckoned him at least a prophet, chose to have him at his feet as a malefactor rather than receive him as a teacher. Robertson and Barnes note the exceeding joy and long curiosity, Wesley that the questions probably concerned his miracles.

The silence is variously explained. Ambrose says he was silent because Herod's unbelief did not deserve to see him and the Lord shunned display, and draws the lesson that when hearers praise us to gain knowledge without amending we ought to be wholly silent, such a hearer always praising what he hears and never following it. Gregory adds that the Redeemer, questioned, held his peace and, expected, disdained to work miracles, preferring to be set at nought by the proud than praised by the hollow. Ellicott observes how little can be said of a silence Luke leaves unexplained, and Gill and Robertson that the questioning got nothing. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott record that the priests stood by accusing him vehemently.

On the robe Clarke argues for a white garment, such as the Jewish nobility wore, Herod mocking after his own country's custom where Pilate's Roman soldiers used purple, and cites Bishop Pearce. Lightfoot would render it white and shining but for Luke's express phrase elsewhere, and takes it for a fool's coat, fitting his suggestion that both rulers thought Jesus deranged. Calvin finds it inevitable that a haughty man should despise one of contemptible appearance, yet allows the pride no excuse, and holds that God purposely hardened him by the spectacle. He notes that Luke names the whole retinue, since the honour due to God is seldom rendered in the courts of kings.

The reconciliation of the rulers divides them most sharply. Ambrose takes the two for a type of Israel and the Gentiles made friends through the Passion, the Gentiles receiving the word first and handing it on to the Jewish people. Bede offers the contrary figure, that the alliance signifies Gentiles and Jews, differing in race, religion and character, agreeing together to persecute Christians. Barnes refuses both, insisting they were not united in hating Jesus, since Pilate wished to release him and both regarded him merely as an object of sport, though wicked men at variance in all else are often united against religion. Both report the conjecture that the old quarrel arose from the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices, Clarke warning that the moderns' guesses are only guesses; Henry recalls how much Herod had heard of Jesus, and Cyril of Jerusalem sets the transfer under the prophecy of one carried bound as a present to a king.
13:
Augustine notes that Luke here returns to the business before the governor after the Herod digression, and infers that he has omitted Pilate's asking our Lord what he had to answer his accusers. Ambrose states the paradox plainly, that Pilate, who as judge acquits Christ, is made the minister of his crucifixion, both rulers refusing to pronounce him guilty while Pilate for fear's sake gratifies their cruelty. Theophylact makes the double acquittal a legal point, that by the testimony of two men Jesus is declared innocent while his accusers produce no credible witness, so that truth triumphs when the accused is silent and not one of the criers corroborates the clamour. Henry presses the inconsistency, that if Pilate believed him innocent he ought to have released him at once.

Robertson notes that Pilate called rulers and people together, Gill and Barnes that he repeated the charge in their own words, and Clarke that he found their accusations frivolous to the last degree. Clarke adds that Herod could best judge whether sedition had been raised among the Galileans, and records the variant which makes Herod send him back to us rather than Pilate send you to him. Ellicott and Robertson report the same reading, and Clarke prefers nothing worthy of death committed by him to done unto him. Wesley marks the proposal to chastise as the point where Pilate begins to give way.

The offer to scourge is condemned by every witness who touches it. Barnes says it is not easy to see why a man who believed Jesus innocent should propose to whip him, and supposes he hoped to conciliate the accusers by a spectacle of disgrace, adding that a Roman magistrate might punish lightly where a grave charge was not made out. Ellicott traces the word from the correction of children to the Roman scourge and finds Pilate halting between two opinions, and Robertson gives the same force. Calvin is harshest, that Pilate acts unjustly in punishing one he has declared blameless, and explains it by the habit of men who commit small injuries under compulsion and then claim the praise of mildness. He adds that had the Son of God been dismissed so he would have carried the shame of scourging without advantage to our salvation, whereas on the cross, as in a chariot, he triumphed over his enemies and ours.

Calvin then turns the scene on his own age, and charges judges who shrink from blood yet scourge Christ himself by compelling the faithful to deny the gospel to save their lives. On the custom of releasing a prisoner Clarke and Ellicott agree that it bound Pilate by no imperial decree but by an annual usage of the nation, and Ellicott weighs whether the verse belongs to the text. Ambrose finds it fitting that men demanding the death of the innocent should seek pardon for a murderer, since such are the laws of iniquity that what innocence hates guilt loves. He presses the name, that Barabbas means son of a father, so that those told they were of their father the devil are figured preferring the son of their father to the true Son of God.

Gill, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson set out the record of Barabbas, a man imprisoned for insurrection and murder, Ellicott noting that Luke alone gives the ground of it. Robertson marks the shouting and the pressing with loud voices, Clarke that Pilate protested a third time, and Wesley that it only sharpened the cry. Barnes and Robertson call the sentence a formal judicial act, Gill and Ellicott describe the exchange by which the murderer was released and Jesus delivered to their will. Cyril of Alexandria's homily here still runs on the accusations rather than the sentence, and Cyril of Jerusalem takes the passage as ground for glorying in the Cross.
26:
The Gloss marks the transition to the crucifixion, and preserves the harmonising note that John has Jesus bearing his own cross out of the city while Simon was pressed into service on the road. Theophylact explains why the burden fell on a stranger, that no one else would take wood counted an abomination; yet he finds in it the prophecy that the government should be upon his shoulder, the cross being Christ's government, worn as other men wear a belt for a mark of dignity. Christ reigns in us only by hardships, he concludes, which is why the luxurious are enemies of his cross. Bede reads the names, Simon meaning obedient and Cyrene an heir, so that the man denotes the Gentiles who, once aliens, have by obedience been made heirs of God.

Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson keep to the plain account, a passer-by from the country seized and the cross laid on him to carry after Jesus. Wesley adds only that the cross was laid on him, Robertson that the imperfect shows the great company following on. Ellicott takes the women's mourning for genuine grief rather than formal. Calvin allows that some still lamented though the whole people had joined in the fury, and Henry distinguishes the mourners from the clamourers.

The turn to the daughters of Jerusalem draws the sharpest comment. Clarke uses it to correct a piety he thinks mistaken, that devout persons are distressed at being unable to weep over the Passion, whereas no human spirit can share sufferings only God manifest in the flesh could bear, which are matter not of sorrow but of rejoicing to a lost world. He names the legend of the stigmata and the hymns that ask one drop of that cup, and answers that one drop would bear the soul down to endless ruin. Calvin takes the words differently, that Christ does not reprove the women but warns them of far greater cause to come, his death being not the end but the beginning of evils to that nation. The words prove, he adds, with what fortitude Christ advanced to death, the punishment which followed showing his life dear to the Father when all thought him forsaken.

Barnes and Ellicott explain the beatitude on the barren as an inversion of a Jewish mother's hope, childlessness becoming a mercy when children could only be a grief. Robertson calls it a beatitude turned upside down, Gill refers the whole to the siege. Lightfoot pursues the cry to the mountains into the Apocalypse, where the same words are said, and infers that the chapter treats of the plagues before the fall of Jerusalem. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley refer the cry to the siege rather than the last judgment, while Henry allows it a further reach in the damnation of sinners.

On the green tree and the dry all take the saying as proverbial and none reads it alike. Barnes explains that a green tree is not easily fired and a dry one burns quickly, so that if the Romans do this to the innocent no security remains for a guilty nation, and applies the figure also to the wicked hereafter, an innocent sufferer having neither remorse nor eternity against him. Clarke turns it the other way, that if men spare not a tree worth preserving for its fruit, the withered one will surely be cut down. Ellicott and Robertson keep to the historical reference, and Calvin makes the sentence confirm the warning, that God would never have permitted his Son such a death but for an expiation of the world's sins. Gill, Lightfoot and Wesley read the green tree of Christ and the dry of the nation left to burn.
32:
Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson agree that the two led out with him were malefactors, Clarke pressing the Greek to show that Luke does not call Jesus another of the same kind, and Robertson noting the imperfect of the leading away. Henry finds in the company the fulfilment of the word that he was numbered with the transgressors, and that he was not only treated as one but ranked among them. Cyril of Alexandria's homily here still runs on the sentence rather than the crucifixion. On the place, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson agree that Calvary is simply the skull, Ellicott adding that the English name comes through the Latin and that the Greek gives no ground for the popular picture of a hill.

Why the place was so named divides the ancients. Athanasius reports the Jewish opinion that Calvary was Adam's burial-place, so that where corruption had been seen incorruption might spring up. Bede offers the plainer account, that outside the gate lay the places where criminals were beheaded, and draws the moral that the innocent was crucified among the guilty so that where sin abounded grace might much more abound. Ellicott prefers the shape or use of the ground to any legend.

Athanasius defends this particular death at length. He argues that the Saviour came to accomplish not his own death but man's, and did not put off the body by sickness, since one who healed others should not be visited with disease; nor could he die privately, for death must precede resurrection and a secret death would have invited every calumny. To the objection that he might have chosen a more glorious end he answers that this would have left him suspected of lacking power over every kind of death, whereas the champion who lays low whatever the enemy sets against him is shown superior to all. He adds that the cross was chosen as the most shameful and accursed death so that in destroying it the dominion of death might be overthrown, and that the body was kept entire, neither beheaded like John's nor sawn asunder like Isaiah's, lest it excuse those who would divide the Church.

Athanasius reads the outstretched hands as drawing the ancient people with one and the Gentiles with the other, and the death in the air as purging it of evil spirits. Gregory of Nyssa takes the figure itself, a cross branching from one centre into four terminations signifying the power of him who hung on it reaching everywhere; his block adds the four dimensions, the crosspiece for good works, the length for perseverance, the height for hope, and the part hidden in the ground for the depth of unmerited grace. Cyril of Alexandria states the christological rule that the only-begotten suffered not in the nature in which he is God but in his earthly nature, so that of one and the same Son both may be affirmed. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the whole scene as the ground of the Church's glorying.

Bede reads the two robbers allegorically, as those who under the faith of Christ undergo martyrdom or a stricter continence, the one seeking eternal glory imitating the thief on the right and the one seeking men's praise the thief on the left. Gregory of Nyssa's block also carries the observation that the thieves were set beside him that he might share their reproach, and that it did not so turn out, since nothing is said of them while his cross is everywhere honoured. Henry keeps to the history, that he was nailed to the cross as it lay upon the ground, and marvels that such barbarity was shown to one against whom nothing was proved. Gill and Barnes note the position between the two, and Ellicott that Luke alone records their being led out with him.
34:
Chrysostom sets the prayer against the Lord's own command, that having told us to pray for our persecutors he did it himself on the cross, not because he could not pardon them but to teach us to pray so in deed as well as word. He limits the petition, that it asks forgiveness if they should repent, Christ being gracious to the penitent who will wash away their guilt by faith. The catena adds that he obtained the fruit of his prayer in those who believed after the Passion, and that he prayed not for men who chose to crucify rather than confess him, but for such as had a zeal for God without knowledge. Against any wider extension it adds that those who remained in unbelief afterwards cannot plead ignorance, the miracles having proclaimed him aloud.

Who exactly was prayed for divides the moderns. Barnes takes it for a fulfilment of the prophecy of intercession for transgressors and applies it to Romans and Jews together, the soldiers being ignorant that he was the Son of God, the Jews knowing him innocent yet not knowing what judgments they brought on their country. Ellicott narrows it, the primary objects being the soldiers who nailed him, since Pilate knew he had condemned the innocent and the priests sinned against light, though he allows an ultimate extension to all who sin without knowing. Robertson agrees that the prayer is for the soldiers and not the Sanhedrin, and warns that some of the oldest documents omit the verse, while holding words so unlike anyone else certainly authentic. Clarke turns the ground of the plea into a rule, weighing how far ignorance excuses.

Calvin finds in the words the proof that Christ was the lamb led out to be sacrificed, since he not only abstained from revenge but pleaded for the salvation of those who tormented him. He notes that Peter proposes this forbearance as the pattern of our patience, and that merely to refrain from cursing would have been much. Gill and Wesley set the prayer first among the seven words, Wesley observing that our Lord passed most of his time on the cross in prayer. Ambrose turns to the manner of the ascent, that he sees him naked, and draws the lesson that whoever would overcome the world should seek none of its appliances.

He presses the figure, that Adam was overcome seeking a covering while Christ overcame by laying his aside, entering paradise as the first man had dwelt in it; and that in laying aside the royal garments he showed he suffered not as God but as man, though Christ is both. His block carries the further reading that he who took all our conditions put on our garments, the signs of Adam's death, to put them off and clothe us with incorruption. Theophylact asks what the soldiers wanted with such clothes, and answers that many were in want, or rather that they did it as a reproach. The catena adds that the lot commends the grace of God, since where a lot is cast we yield not to merit but to God's secret judgment.

Lightfoot goes after the seamless coat, reporting the tradition that Moses ministered through the seven days of consecration in a white vestment without a seam, made of one thread and not, as our clothes are, with the sleeves sewn on. He records with contempt the reason given for its seamlessness, that Moses might not be suspected of hiding consecrated money in the seams. Robertson and Barnes refer the casting of lots to John's fuller account, where four soldiers divide the rest and cast for the coat alone. Gill and Ellicott note the parting of the raiment as fulfilling the psalm, and Clarke that the soldiers acted by custom and not malice.
35:
Ellicott notes that Luke uses the generic term for the Sanhedrin where Matthew particularises, and that the verb for their derision implies the curled lip of scorn. He hears in the taunt that he saved others an unconscious prophecy after the manner of Caiaphas, and observes that this is the only place in the New Testament where the adjective chosen is applied directly to Christ. Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson set out the scene plainly, the people beholding while the rulers scoffed, Clarke calling it the utmost contempt. Wesley marks the parallel between the rulers' challenge to the Christ and the soldiers' to the king of the Jews.

Lightfoot turns aside to the vinegar, showing that it was the common drink of Roman soldiers, always at hand where crucified men were kept, and citing the discipline forbidding wine on campaign and the provisioning of frontier cities. He uses this to reconcile the evangelists, proposing wine mingled with myrrh given by the Jews before the nailing and vinegar by the soldiers afterwards, and adds that if a third cup be granted all difficulty vanishes. Ellicott reads the offer more gently, that the soldiers still knew not what they did, and that some rough kindliness may have mingled with the mockery. Clarke and Robertson refer it to the fuller accounts in the other Gospels, and Gill takes the soldiers' words as a taunt drawn from the title over his head.

On that title Theophylact sees the devil's device turned a second time against himself, the accusation being published in three characters so that no passer-by could miss why he was crucified. He presses the choice of tongues, the most powerful of nations, the wisest, and those who most worshipped God being thereby signified subject to the dominion of Christ. Ambrose finds the title rightly placed above the cross, since Christ's kingdom is not of the human body but of the power of God, and reads it against two other texts, the King of the Jews against my kingdom is not of this world, and the cause written above his head against the Word was God. Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson keep to the history of the inscription, Gill and Wesley to its wording.

The catena's comment here runs on past the title to the penitent thief, so that the fathers keyed at this verse already expound what follows. Chrysostom makes the condemned man perform the office of judge, one who before Pilate confessed only after many tortures now deciding concerning truth, and distinguishes the confession that brings punishment from the confession made to salvation. He sets the rebuke of his fellow as a lesson to the bystanders, and when their ears were stopped the thief turned to him who knows the heart, seeing a hidden kingdom in one who wore the form of a condemned criminal. Gregory observes that nails had fastened hands and feet so that nothing remained free but heart and tongue, and that the thief offered God the whole of what he found free, believing with the heart and confessing with the mouth.

He adds that the thief received on the cross all three virtues the Apostle names, faith in believing that one dying beside him would reign, hope in asking entrance to that kingdom, and charity in reproving his fellow. Ambrose takes the exchange as a remarkable example of conversion, the Lord pardoning quickly because the thief is quickly converted, and grace being more abundant than prayer, since he asked only to be remembered and was answered with paradise. Theophylact adds the figure of a victorious king carrying the best of his spoils in triumph, the Lord having despoiled the devil of part of his plunder. Gregory of Nyssa's block at this key likewise turns to the thief rather than the title.
39:
Barnes begins with the discrepancy, that Matthew says the thieves cast the same in his teeth where Luke distinguishes them; Ellicott gives the same account and Robertson marks the imperfect of the railing. Barnes reads the impenitent man's prayer sharply, that he sought deliverance from the cross and not from his sins, which is why he was not heard, and compares men who pray earnestly in sickness and forget it on recovery. Calvin observes that a reproach from a fellow-sufferer completed his abasement, and Wesley marks the change from the plural of the other evangelists to the singular. Leo, following the Passion through a course of sermons, finds the two robbers displaying the difference that must be made among all men, the believing thief a type of those to be saved and the blasphemer of those to be damned.

Clarke takes the rebuke as evidence that suffering had wrought on one and not the other, and Gill and Barnes press the question whether a man so near death should not fear God. Ellicott collects the legends, that the penitent was named Dysmas and had once attacked the holy family in flight, so that he now recognised the face; but he sets these aside and keeps to what Luke records. He finds the man impressed by the holiness and patience of the sufferer, so that words uttered in mockery became an element in his conversion, and locates the root deeper in a fear of God whose absence he noted in his companion. He adds that in accepting his punishment as just he made it reformatory and not merely penal, which Robertson and Barnes echo on the due reward of their deeds.

Calvin makes this the centre of the chapter, knowing no more remarkable example of faith since the creation of the world. He wonders that a robber never in Christ's school should rise higher than all the apostles, adoring as king one who hung on a gallows and calling the dying man the Author of life. He asks what marks of royalty such a man could have seen, and answers that his mind's eyes must have been acute to behold life in death, glory in shame and victory in destruction. He turns it against his readers, that if a robber raised the crucified Christ to a heavenly throne, woe to our sloth if we do not reverence him at God's right hand; and he traces the thief's assurance to his seeing in that death a sacrifice able to expiate the sins of the world.

Lightfoot approaches the answer through the word paradise, showing from rabbinic usage that it meant the garden of Eden, and reporting the tradition of the four who entered it. Ellicott traces the same word from a Persian term for a king's enclosed park, adopted by the Greek translators, into Jewish and Christian usage. Clarke reports that Marcion and the Manichees left the verse out, and takes the saying for a strong proof of the soul's immateriality. He then attacks the expedient of placing a comma after today, so that the sense becomes I tell thee this today, and is sorry to find men of learning supporting so feeble a criticism, which a good cause cannot need.

Barnes doubts that the day can be pushed to the resurrection, and Robertson gives the plain construction. Gill and Wesley define paradise as the place where the souls of the righteous wait, and Ellicott asks whether it is heaven itself. Calvin observes that Christ had not yet entered his kingdom publicly and yet gave more than was asked, and Cyril of Jerusalem asks the robber directly what power led him to so great a confession. Lightfoot and Barnes note that the promise is peculiar to Luke, Gill that Jesus answered immediately.
44:
Cyril of Alexandria reads the darkness as the world bewailing its rightful Master, and the light failing at midday as a token that the souls of the crucifiers would suffer darkness. His block preserves the argument that this was no common eclipse, since Passover falls at full moon and an eclipse only at new; and beside it the report of two observers at Heliopolis who saw the moon meet the sun out of season, light being lost and restored from opposite sides of the diameter. The catena concludes that the miracle was wrought to make known that he who had undergone death was ruler of the whole creation. Ambrose reads it morally instead, the sun eclipsed to the sacrilegious to overshadow their wickedness, and darkness spread over unbelieving eyes that the light of faith might rise.

Bede notices a difficulty of order, that Luke joins the rending of the veil to the darkness where Matthew and Mark place it at the death, and concludes that he relates it by anticipation. Theophylact takes the rending to mean that the Holy of Holies should be inaccessible no longer but given over to the Romans and defiled, and elsewhere that the veil of enmity and sin which kept us from the holy things in heaven is broken through. Ambrose reads in it the division of the two peoples, the old veil rent that the Church might hang up the new walls of faith. Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Wesley keep to the history of the darkness, referring the discussion to the parallel accounts, and Henry observes that it lasted three hours and not three days as in Egypt.

On the loud cry Ambrose finds proof that Christ could lay down his life and take it again, and distinguishes giving up from losing, since what a man sends forth is voluntary and what he loses compulsory. Bede reads the address to the Father as declaring him the Son of God, and the commending of the spirit not as weakness but as confidence in the same power. Chrysostom draws from the words that the souls of the saints are no longer shut up below but are with God, Christ being the beginning of that change. Ambrose adds that the flesh dies that the Spirit may rise, and that heavenly things too may be loosed from the chain of iniquity.

Gregory of Nyssa raises the question the three sayings create, how the Lord distributes himself at once into the heart of the earth, into paradise, and into the Father's hands. He answers that to those who consider rightly it is scarcely a question, since he who by divine power is in every place is present in any place. John Damascene puts the distribution more exactly, that in respect of his body he was in the grave, of his soul in hell, and with the thief in paradise. Gregory of Nyssa adds that his divinity left neither part but separated soul from body of its own accord while abiding in each, so that through the body he vanquished death and through the soul opened paradise to the thief.

Henry treats the darkness as a mourning of nature and a sign that the Sun of righteousness was withdrawing. He reads the loud cry as showing that the agony of his soul was over, and the commending as a surrender into the Father's hand to be received into paradise. Ambrose closes on the reach of it, that though the Spirit is above he gives light to the parts beneath the earth, so that all things may be redeemed. Cyril of Alexandria's second block here is his homily on the crucifixion rather than the death, the catena running a pericope behind.
45:
Robertson prefers the reading of the best manuscripts, that the sun's light failed rather than that it was darkened, and Gill and Clarke refer the cause to fuller discussions elsewhere. Wesley keeps to the plain statement, and Cyril of Jerusalem takes the scene into his catechesis on the garden and the tomb. On the last cry Ellicott and Robertson note that Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips, the evening prayer of every Jewish child, so that he died as a child falls asleep. Clarke observes that the words were spoken in the confidence of one committing a trust, not yielding to necessity, and Barnes that the loud voice showed his strength unspent.

Augustine explains the centurion's marvel from the manner of the death, since crucified men commonly died by a lingering end, whereas this one cried aloud and immediately gave up the ghost, showing what power he had while dying. He then harmonises the accounts, that there is no contradiction between Matthew's earthquake and Luke's death, since Matthew adds the words and at the things that were done, while Luke's phrase gathers all the wonders of that hour into one. Where Matthew has truly this was the Son of God and Luke certainly this was a righteous man, he offers two solutions, that both were spoken and each evangelist reported one, or that Luke gives the sense the centurion meant, since he may have called him the Son of God only because he believed him just, as just men are so called. He adds that Matthew's mention of the centurion's companions and Luke's silence are no contradiction, and that in fearing the man glorified God.

Theophylact finds the promise fulfilled that being lifted up he would draw all men, since from the cross he drew the thief, the centurion and some of the people. Ambrose turns to those not drawn, in an outburst on breasts harder than the rocks, since the judge acquits, the officer believes, the traitor by his death condemns his crime, the earth quakes and the graves open, while that hardness remains immovable though the world is shaken. Gill, Barnes and Robertson keep to the record, Robertson noting that the imperfect shows the centurion kept on glorifying God and Barnes explaining the confession as a Roman soldier could have meant it. Wesley distinguishes those who had been actors in the crime from those who came only to look.

On the smiting of the breasts Ellicott explains that the word for the sight is used of a gathered spectacle, and Clarke that all were deeply affected, though he doubts how deep it went. The catena gives two readings of the gesture, that they bewailed one unjustly slain, or that remembering they had demanded his death they trembled to see him glorified in dying; and it contrasts the Gentiles who glorified God by open confession with those who struck their breasts and went home silent. Barnes and Robertson observe that the crowd which had shouted now went away in another temper, and Gill that the change was short-lived. Ellicott notes that the acquaintance standing afar off is peculiar to Luke, and finds in it the psalm's complaint that friend and neighbour were put far away.

Robertson and Barnes describe the women who had followed from Galilee standing at a distance, and Ellicott identifies them with those named in the next chapter. Gill remarks that they stood as near as they durst, Wesley that they witnessed everything done. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the darkness and the death as the ground of the Church's confession, and Theophylact reads the hour as the beginning of the drawing of the nations. Ambrose closes by making the centurion's faith the faith of the Church, bearing witness to the Son of God in the synagogue's silence.
50:
Bede opens with the office, that a counsellor or decurio is so called from the order of the curia whose business he administers, and identifies Arimathea with the Ramathaim of Elkanah and Samuel. He finds him fitted by his righteousness for the burial and worthy by his rank to obtain it, and draws from its simplicity a rebuke of rich men who cannot be without their wealth even in their graves. The Greek Exposition explains the change, that a secret disciple burst the bonds of fear and grew zealous, gaining a precious jewel by the meekness of his asking. Augustine states the difficulty more sharply, that a secret disciple should dare what none of the open followers dared, and answers that he acted on the confidence of his rank, which gave him familiar entrance to Pilate, and that in this last office he cared less for Jewish hostility.

Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson set out the facts soberly, Robertson noting the double negative by which Luke says he had not consented, and Ellicott that the phrase covers both the decision and its execution, clearing Joseph of the whole proceeding. Wesley remarks that a good and just man was found even in that council, Gill that he was a disciple though secretly. Robertson describes the asking as a formal request granted by the governor, and Barnes the taking down and winding in linen. Ellicott and Robertson note the sepulchre hewn in stone and never yet used.

Lightfoot brings rabbinic background to the linen, that shrouds for those executed by sentence were made from the worn cloths in which the books of the Law had been wrapped, and this to their disgrace. He explains the principle, that the more shamefully a condemned man was handled the greater his supposed atonement, so that such men were wrapped in ragged and dirty windingsheets to augment their expiation. He adds the same rule about lamentation, and observes that any other man might on this reckoning have told the women not to weep lest they cut short his expiation, whereas Christ spoke on another account. Ambrose turns to the mystical sense, that the just man buries the body of Christ and covers it with linen, and bids the reader clothe that body with its own glory so as to become just.

On the hour Lightfoot examines the phrase that the sabbath drew on, and offers two accounts, that it began to shine with the candles every household was bound to light, or that the Jews simply called the evening of a day its light. Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson explain the preparation as the day before the sabbath and weigh how the reckoning bears on the chronology. Lightfoot returns to the question of time, reasoning that if the body was taken down about sunset the women had the interval called between the suns, from sunset to the appearance of a star, in which to buy their spices. Gill and Barnes note that they marked the tomb and how the body was laid, Ellicott that Luke alone follows the women so closely.

Theophylact reads the spices as a measure of their faith, that not yet believing enough they prepared ointments as for a mere man, after the Jewish manner toward their dead. They worked, he observes, as long as it was lawful, and then kept the commanded rest from evening to evening. Ellicott treats that rest and the ointments most fully, and Clarke the custom of embalming and how far the Jews practised it. Henry closes on the burial as the last stage of Christ's humiliation, and takes the women's resting according to the commandment for a sign that the sabbath was still binding, though the day was afterwards altered.
